papers.title: HSI Survey
papers.resume: Scenario: survey of human–swarm interaction research and design issues across multiple swarm tasks and application domains. Human role: describes how a human can command, supervise, and collaborate with swarms under different communication and autonomy assumptions. Interface/support: synthesizes interaction modalities and information needs (e.g., global broadcast, intermittent intervention, environment-based control) and organizes challenges rather than proposing a single UI. Evaluation: systematic literature synthesis (taxonomy-style contribution), not a new experiment. Key claim: a structured view of interaction paradigms clarifies constraints and research gaps for scalable, safe human control of swarms.

papers.title: Interface Insights
papers.resume: Scenario: empirical study that develops and tests a systematic method for designing human–swarm interaction interfaces. Human role: operator supervises and issues commands to a swarm to complete task goals under alternative interface designs. Interface/support: compares UI variants grounded in theoretical HSI insights and extracts concrete interface design insights tied to performance. Evaluation: controlled user study using task-performance measures (e.g., completion time and errors) and participant feedback to compare interface conditions. Key claim: specific interface elements measurably affect operator effectiveness, enabling evidence-based HSI interface design.

papers.title: Runtime PFM
papers.resume: Scenario: human–swarm mission supported by predictive formal modelling (PFM) executed at runtime as decision support. Human role: operator monitors mission state and makes control decisions while supervising a swarm. Interface/support: predictive outputs from formal models are presented to the operator during the mission to inform choices. Evaluation: user study comparing baseline control versus PFM-assisted control on performance and human–swarm interaction outcomes. Key claim: runtime predictive formal modelling can provide measurable benefits to mission performance and interaction quality in HSI.

papers.title: Adaptive Training
papers.resume: Scenario: conceptual analysis of why adaptive operator training is critical for effective human–swarm interaction. Human role: operator must learn swarm dynamics and adapt strategies as mission complexity, automation levels, and swarm behavior change. Interface/support: focuses on training design considerations (what skills to build and how to adapt training) rather than a specific control interface. Evaluation: perspective and synthesis drawing on cognitive systems engineering and systems science; no controlled study reported. Key claim: training should be adaptive to the operator and context to prevent brittle performance and support robust HSI in complex missions.

papers.title: MICAH Indicators
papers.resume: Scenario: review that distills indicators needed to enable adaptive autonomy in human–swarm interaction. Human role: the human’s state (e.g., workload and other human factors) is treated as a key driver for adaptive teaming decisions. Interface/support: proposes the MICAH framework (Mission–Interaction–Complexity–Automation–Human) mapping primitive indicators an adaptive agent should monitor and reason over. Evaluation: literature synthesis and framework proposal; no direct user-study validation described. Key claim: explicitly characterizing mission, interaction, complexity, automation, and human indicators is necessary groundwork for adaptive human–swarm teaming.

papers.title: Heatmap UI
papers.resume: Scenario: single-operator management of a large UAV swarm through a user-centered control interface. Human role: operator monitors the swarm and issues controls to manage many UAVs as a coherent team. Interface/support: interactive interface derived from user preferences; heat-map visualization of the swarm is highlighted as improving usability and acceptance. Evaluation: user studies including a 100-participant study and an additional complementary study to evaluate the interface and control mechanism. Key claim: representing the swarm as a heat map supports more usable and acceptable single-operator management of scalable UAV swarms.

papers.title: AR Remote HSI
papers.resume: Scenario: remote human–swarm interaction where a person controls a robot team through a video call, comparing AR versus non-AR interfaces. Human role: remote operator commands the robot team and monitors progress via the communication channel. Interface/support: a simple augmented-reality overlay interface is contrasted with an unaugmented baseline display. Evaluation: remote human user studies comparing the two interfaces on effectiveness and user experience during control. Key claim: AR-based interface support can improve remote HSI effectiveness relative to an unaugmented interface in the studied setting.

papers.title: HotL Explanations
papers.resume: Scenario: supervision of small UAV swarms where autonomous behaviors require explanations to maintain operator awareness in human-on-the-loop control. Human role: operator monitors multiple sUAS, stays aware of autonomy decisions, and intervenes when needed. Interface/support: analyzes UI trade-offs for providing timely versus detailed explanations and proposes a HotL multi-sUAS interface design with guidelines. Evaluation: multiple user studies with both inexperienced and expert operators assessing interface choices and their impact on awareness and interaction. Key claim: explanation timing and granularity materially affect operator awareness, motivating specific design guidelines for explanatory swarm interfaces.

papers.title: Fan-Out Model
papers.resume: Scenario: scalability modeling for human multi-robot teams, revisiting fan-out to address limitations of prior neglect-time formulations. Human role: operator supervises multiple robots and forms estimates of how long each can operate without attention. Interface/support: introduces a fan-out model that decomposes neglect time into robot self-sufficient time and the human’s estimate of that self-sufficiency. Evaluation: model formulation and evaluation against existing modeling approaches to improve predictive accuracy. Key claim: explicitly separating robot capability from human estimation yields a more accurate scalability model for human–robot team supervision.

papers.title: HORUS MR
papers.resume: Scenario: user study where participants manage a team of mobile robots tasked with finding clues in an environment that simulates search-and-rescue. Human role: operator coordinates multiple robots either through team-level management or through individual robot teleoperation. Interface/support: HORUS provides a mixed-reality interface enabling full-team management and coordination, contrasted with teleoperation. Evaluation: experiments compare HORUS to teleoperation on task effectiveness and multi-robot coordination capability. Key claim: mixed-reality team-level interaction can increase versatility and effectiveness of multi-robot management compared with individual teleoperation.

papers.title: SA+TP Framework
papers.resume: Scenario: single-target search in a dynamic grid where operators guide a robotic swarm and mark hazardous cells that the swarm does not know. Human role: operator directs swarm movement and provides hazard annotations during the search. Interface/support: tablet-based interface operationalizes the proposed framework and supports simultaneous measurement of SA and task performance. Evaluation: user study using subjective and objective SA measures; performance is quantified by how close robots are to the target. Key claim: the framework enables consistent HSI study design and links SA measurements to measurable search-task performance.
papers.sa2_how: SA2 is supported by explicitly measuring comprehension-level situation awareness during the task using complementary subjective and objective SA instruments, not only perception or outcomes.

papers.title: Two Types HSI
papers.resume: Scenario: foraging swarm target-search comparing intermittent interaction and environmental interaction, instantiated as selection control and beacon control. Human role: operator steers the foraging swarm to find targets via direct selection actions or by placing environmental beacons. Interface/support: provides both control methods to study how different interaction structures shape swarm behavior and operator effectiveness. Evaluation: controlled experimental comparison of the two interaction types on foraging task performance. Key claim: fundamental differences between intermittent and environmental interaction lead to different operator strategies and performance in foraging control.

papers.title: Limited SA HSI
papers.resume: Scenario: simulated human–swarm collaboration when the operator’s situational awareness is intentionally limited. Human role: operator must decide how to influence the swarm while lacking full visibility of swarm and environment state. Interface/support: investigates interaction under constrained feedback, focusing on how the available information and controls shape collaboration. Evaluation: simulation-based study assessing task outcomes and interaction behavior in limited-awareness conditions. Key claim: limited situational awareness substantially changes how operators can collaborate with swarms, motivating interaction designs robust to partial observability.

papers.title: HST3 Architecture
papers.resume: Scenario: conceptual work proposing an architecture that links transparency to trustworthy human–swarm teaming. Human role: operator requires transparency to maintain situational awareness and properly calibrate trust in swarm autonomy. Interface/support: defines transparency as overarching and organizes interpretability, explainability, and predictability within the HST3-Architecture. Evaluation: definition-driven synthesis and architecture proposal; no empirical evaluation is described in the provided summary. Key claim: structuring transparency mechanisms is a prerequisite for situation awareness and thus for effective, trustworthy human–swarm teaming. It emphasizes transparency mechanisms across system and UI layers.
papers.sa2_how: SA2 is supported by prioritizing transparency content that conveys meaning, intent, and predictability of swarm behavior so the human can understand what is happening and why.

papers.title: Hybrid MR Arch
papers.resume: Scenario: hybrid robotic swarm architecture that combines virtual and physical components into a virtual–physical simulation system. Human role: operator interacts with the hybrid swarm and monitors both virtual and physical elements during experimentation. Interface/support: mixed-reality devices provide an MR user interface integrated into the system architecture to enable human–swarm interaction. Evaluation: system architecture and prototype demonstration emphasizing integration; no user-study metrics are stated in the provided summary. Key claim: integrating MR interaction with virtual–physical hybrid swarm simulation broadens experimental capability for HSI and swarm system development.

papers.title: Influence Moderation
papers.resume: Scenario: simulated human–swarm system inspired by honeybees, used to study how to moderate human influence over swarm outcomes. Human role: operator interacts with the swarm under different designs that constrain or shape the impact of human inputs. Interface/support: implements multiple moderation methods that regulate how operator commands affect the swarm, aiming to prevent harmful over-influence. Evaluation: simulation study comparing mission success across influence-moderation approaches using the same swarm task. Key claim: appropriately moderating human influence can improve overall system success, suggesting design principles for balancing guidance and swarm autonomy.

papers.title: Immersion+Prediction
papers.resume: Scenario: multi-robot operation comparing four interfaces that vary immersion (VR vs conventional) and prediction (predictive vs non-predictive). Human role: operator controls and supervises multiple robots while maintaining situational awareness. Interface/support: implements conventional, predictive conventional, VR, and predictive VR interfaces, emphasizing multimodal interaction, immersion, and predictive capabilities. Evaluation: comparative study focusing on operator situational awareness under the four interface designs. Key claim: immersion and prediction features are key levers for improving operator situational awareness in multi-robot control interfaces. It also discusses adaptive displays combining immersion and prediction.
papers.sa2_how: SA2 is supported by predictive interface elements and immersive context that help the operator interpret robot states and their implications, supporting comprehension beyond raw perception.

papers.title: xSwarm Space
papers.resume: Scenario: requirements study on explainability for swarm robotics, targeting safety-critical contexts where humans must control and monitor swarms. Human role: operator needs answers and explanations to support trustworthy supervision and intervention. Interface/support: frames the xSwarm design space by identifying what questions an explainable swarm should answer and what types of explanations it should generate. Evaluation: survey of 26 swarm experts to elicit explainability requirements and challenges in producing explanations. Key claim: current HSI literature lacks foundational explainability requirements, and expert-elicited needs can guide development of explainable swarm systems.

papers.title: SAT Model
papers.resume: Scenario: extension of the Situation Awareness-based Agent Transparency (SAT) model to support advanced human–autonomy teaming paradigms. Human role: human teammate must maintain appropriate understanding and calibrated trust in agent judgment as autonomy becomes a teammate. Interface/support: argues for bidirectional transparency and illustrates the model in three programs (autonomous squad member, mediator for multiple robots, plan recommendation agent). Evaluation: review of the model’s application across these programs to demonstrate utility, not a single new experiment. Key claim: SAT remains effective for facilitating shared understanding and trust calibration, and its extension better supports teamwork with autonomous teammates.
papers.sa2_how: SA2 is supported by SAT’s guidance to communicate the meaning and implications of agent state and intent, enabling human comprehension rather than only exposing raw data.

papers.title: Runtime Verification
papers.resume: Scenario: runtime probabilistic modelling and verification used as formal-methods support to aid operator situational awareness in swarm missions. Human role: operator monitors the system and considers decisions using current and predictive success information. Interface/support: probabilistic models compute task and mission success probabilities; statistical model checking provides timely approximate predictions and enables what-if exploration before acting. Evaluation: reports prediction performance (timeliness and approximation accuracy) and implements approaches to display outputs to operators. Key claim: runtime formal verification can provide actionable insight into current and future mission success to support better operator decisions.

papers.title: OODA Framework
papers.resume: Scenario: single-operator control of more than 20 UAVs using a human-centered HSI framework grounded in the OODA cognitive model. Human role: operator follows observe–orient–decide–act workflows to manage UAV swarm missions while limiting cognitive load. Interface/support: six HSI-adapted design principles guide system development across interaction workflows, interface layout, and task representation mechanisms in a prototype. Evaluation: user studies evaluating usability, interaction efficiency, and cognitive support; results suggest reduced cognitive load and improved control performance with remaining UI refinements needed. Key claim: an OODA-grounded framework can guide interface design that supports scalable, cognitively manageable UAV swarm supervision.
papers.sa2_how: SA2 is supported by the OODA ‘orient’ stage operationalized in the interface workflow and task representations, aiming to improve operator understanding before decisions and actions.

papers.title: SA Training Proposal
papers.resume: Scenario: human–autonomy teaming under high complexity where time pressure, task load, and fatigue hinder forming sound predictions. Human role: soldiers/operators collaborate with an uncrewed swarm system for ISR and must adjust collaboration mode as the environment changes. Interface/support: proposes preparation and training to empower humans to make projections and manage collaboration, and outlines non-interventional and interventional techniques for studying SA in teams operating the UxS. Evaluation: demonstration and experiment proposal rather than completed study; intended measures are described conceptually in the paper summary. Key claim: situation awareness training is a prerequisite for handling complexity in human–autonomy teams and for effective joint projection of future events.

papers.title: SwarmControl Online
papers.resume: Scenario: massive online user study using SwarmControl.net, where players steer swarms of up to 500 robots in manipulation challenges. Human role: remote users act as swarm operators, learning strategies to control large robot populations through the game interface. Interface/support: web-based game framework designed for large-scale HSI experiments and released as an open-source tool for running swarm manipulation studies. Evaluation: logs and analyzes statistics from thousands of players to study large-population control behaviors and pitfalls. Key claim: crowdsourced online games can enable unprecedented scale in swarm-manipulation experimentation and produce data useful for both human control insights and automatic controller design.

papers.title: SHMM Updates
papers.resume: Scenario: human–robot interaction when continuous monitoring is unavailable, requiring selective communication about state and plans. Human role: operator maintains a mental model of world state and robot plans and risks divergence from the robot’s actual state. Interface/support: framework estimates the operator’s mental model and compares it with the true world state and robot plans; mismatches trigger selective communication updates. Evaluation: presents a planning and communication framework; specific user-study metrics are not stated in the provided summary. Key claim: explicitly modelling and tracking the operator’s mental model enables targeted communication that can reduce unnecessary updates while keeping the human aligned with real-time robot planning.

papers.title: OFFSET Field Study
papers.resume: Scenario: DARPA OFFSET program field exercises at urban training sites assessing single-operator supervision of a heterogeneous swarm of 100 robots in real-world missions. Human role: swarm commander deploys and supervises the heterogeneous swarm during challenging operational missions. Interface/support: uses the CCAST integrator team’s command-and-control setup to manage the swarm (specific UI elements are not detailed in the provided summary). Evaluation: collects objective and subjective human-performance metrics and analyzes workload using a multi-dimensional workload algorithm with an overload threshold. Key claim: despite workload frequently exceeding overload thresholds, the swarm commander successfully completed missions, demonstrating feasibility of single-human supervision for 100 heterogeneous robots in real-world conditions.

papers.title: VR Drone UI Eval
papers.resume: Scenario: VR-based evaluation of drone swarm control systems and interfaces in a virtual search-and-rescue operation. Human role: participant controls a drone swarm through candidate control systems while performing SAR tasks in VR. Interface/support: VR environment supports user-centered design and rapid prototyping of drone swarm behaviors and control interfaces. Evaluation: situational awareness measured with SART, usability measured with SUS (for VR system and control systems), simulator sickness measured with SSQ, plus performance metrics and qualitative feedback. Key claim: VR is a viable platform for evaluating swarm control systems and interfaces with complementary SA, performance, usability, and comfort measures.

papers.title: Neglect Benevolence
papers.resume: Scenario: swarm foraging under feedback latency, examining how delayed swarm-state feedback affects control and whether predictive displays mitigate it. Human role: operator commands the swarm to find targets and must decide when to intervene versus allowing swarm behaviors to stabilize. Interface/support: compares conditions with and without a predictive display and introduces ‘neglect benevolence’ to capture benefits of waiting for stabilization before issuing new commands. Evaluation: controlled study measuring target-search task performance across latency and display conditions and analyzing emergent operator strategies. Key claim: predictive displays can reduce negative latency effects, and operators exploit neglect benevolence through different but successful control strategies.

papers.title: Two Types Study
papers.resume: Scenario: foraging swarm target-search comparing intermittent interaction and environmental interaction, implemented as selection control and beacon control. Human role: operator directs the swarm to locate targets by selecting entities/actions or by placing beacons that influence collective motion. Interface/support: experimental interface exposes both control paradigms so the same task can be performed under different interaction structures. Evaluation: controlled experiment comparing interaction types on foraging task performance and operator behavior. Key claim: interaction structure (selection vs beacon) shapes successful strategies and provides evidence that intermittent and environmental control support different forms of effective human–swarm coordination.

papers.title: VR Training Sim
papers.resume: Scenario: VR-based UAV simulator for immersive training and cognitive evaluation in rescue and emergency missions using a leader–follower drone setup. Human role: trainee/operator pilots a lead drone via VR headset and joystick while autonomous drones maintain geometric formations with sensing and obstacle avoidance. Interface/support: immersive VR training environment couples human piloting with autonomy-managed formation control to practice swarm leadership. Evaluation: simulator is presented for training and human-factors assessment; specific quantitative study outcomes are not stated in the provided summary. Key claim: an immersive VR simulator can support operator training and cognitive evaluation for UAV swarm control in safety-relevant mission contexts.
